title: Deterministic query complexity of tournament kings
formal: Determine the asymptotic order of \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\), the minimum worst-case number of edge-orientation queries needed by a deterministic decision tree to output one king of every tournament on \([n]\). The domain is the integers \(n\ge 2\). The required precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to absolute constant factors: supply a positive function \(f\) and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge 2\) such that \(c f(n)\le D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\le C f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\).
why: This is a longstanding total search problem in which existence is elementary but the information needed for deterministic discovery is unresolved. It isolates a substantial gap between deterministic and randomized access to a graph, without the computational cost of processing already known edges. A tight bound would explain how much pairwise information is inherently required to identify a vertex with global two-step reachability, a tournament solution motivated by pairwise competition and social choice.
status_note: The FSTTCS 2025 paper explicitly leaves this deterministic gap open. The original bounds and the 2022–2024 related results were checked against primary papers. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified improvement settling the target; this is a bounded search, not an independent verification of all proofs or an exhaustive current-status certification.

progress.text: Shen, Sheng and Wu prove an \(O(n^{3/2})\) upper bound and an \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) lower bound for finding one king. Their matching \(\Theta(n^{3/2})\) result concerns a sorted sequence of kings and does not close the single-output gap.

Lachish, Reidl and Trehan obtain \(O(n^{4/3}\operatorname{polylog} n)\) queries for a vertex that reaches at least a \(1/2+2/17\) fraction of all vertices within two steps. The fraction is strictly below one.

Mande, Paraashar and Saurabh prove randomized bounds between \(\Omega(n)\) and \(O(n\log\log n)\), and quantum bounds matching up to polylogarithmic factors around \(\sqrt n\), with bounded error. These do not alter the deterministic bounds.
Abboud, Grossman, Naor and Solomon give a zero-error randomized algorithm using at most \(2n\) queries in expectation. Their Question 7 separately restates the unresolved deterministic gap.

Ismaili Alaoui and Mande prove \(\Theta(n^2)\) randomized query complexity for king existence in general digraphs and for strong-king search in tournaments. Their concluding Section 5 again identifies ordinary deterministic king search as open with the 2003 bounds.

importance.reason: A well-established query-complexity gap for a canonical total graph search problem, with a pronounced deterministic–randomized distinction and sustained independent work since 2003.

sentences: A king in a tournament reaches every other vertex along a directed path of at most two edges.
A deterministic algorithm learns the orientation of one chosen edge per query and must output a king for every tournament.
The target is its optimal worst-case query count up to constant factors as the number of vertices grows.
The checked deterministic bounds remain \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) and \(O(n^{3/2})\), whereas randomization permits linear expected query cost.
Closing the deterministic gap would quantify how much pairwise information this total search task inherently requires.

definitions: A tournament on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a loopless directed graph having exactly one of the arcs \(i\to j\) and \(j\to i\) for each distinct pair. Represent it by a bit \(x_{ij}\) for each \(1\le i<j\le n\): value 1 means \(i\to j\), and value 0 means \(j\to i\). Every assignment of these \(\binom n2\) bits is a valid input; there are no transitivity, degree or distribution promises. A vertex \(v\) is a king if for every \(u\ne v\), either \(v\to u\), or there exists \(w\in[n]\setminus\{u,v\}\) with \(v\to w\) and \(w\to u\). Thus the path must follow the arrows and have at most two edges. The task is to output any one such vertex, rather than to decide whether one exists, to verify a given candidate, or to output every king. A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node names a pair \(i<j\), its two outgoing edges are labeled 0 and 1, and each leaf names one vertex. Starting at the root, the input follows the edge matching the named input bit. The tree is correct if the leaf reached is a king for every complete bit assignment. Its cost is the maximum number of internal nodes visited over all inputs. Define \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\) as the minimum cost of a correct tree for that n. The tree may choose later queries from previous answers. Only single-edge queries are charged; internal computation, storage, knowledge of n and production of the vertex label are free. Separate trees may be chosen for each n; no polynomial-time construction or uniform generation of their descriptions is required. There are no random coins, quantum queries or additional graph oracles. Every nonempty tournament has a king, so this minimum is finite; the omitted one-vertex case has cost zero. Constants in the asymptotic answer are independent of n and of the tournament, and logarithmic factors are not absorbed into those constants.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked characterization of \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\) to the stated constant-factor precision. An acceptable positive function \(f\) must be specified by an unambiguous mathematical description and accompanied by proofs of both bounds for every sufficiently large integer n in the stated decision-tree model. The upper bound must establish correct trees at all such sizes; the lower bound must apply to every correct tree. Merely renaming the defining minimum, bounding only its exponent while leaving nonconstant factors unspecified, or improving just one side of the gap does not meet this criterion. This is an asymptotic target, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance is not an additive tolerance on its growth rate.

context_blocks.text: Pairwise outcomes can cycle: one player defeats a second, the second defeats a third, and the third defeats the first. A king need not defeat everyone directly; it must defeat each other player either directly or through one intermediary. In that three-cycle all three vertices qualify. The task therefore allows multiple correct outputs and does not impose an ordering or tie-breaking rule.

The graph is hidden behind edge queries. Reading its entire adjacency table always supplies enough information, but a search algorithm may stop once the answers force one output vertex to be a king in every tournament consistent with them. The central question is the optimal amount of information for this search relation, with unrestricted computation on what has been learned.

The source asks to determine the deterministic complexity without proposing a particular exponent as the answer. This card makes the requested asymptotic precision explicit as \(\Theta\), preserving the full gap question. An upper bound of \(O(n^{4/3})\) or a lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2})\) would match a known opposite bound, but neither exponent is imposed as the conjectured answer.

A zero-error randomized algorithm can have a small expected number of queries while some random outcomes use more. A bounded-error randomized algorithm instead permits a small failure probability on each fixed tournament. Both differ from the deterministic worst-case target. Similarly, reaching a fixed fraction of vertices is a weaker output requirement than being a king.

The 2025 paper resolves two nearby questions: deciding king existence in arbitrary directed graphs, and finding a strong king in a tournament. A strong king satisfies an additional comparison between numbers of two-edge paths in opposite directions. Neither result gives the optimum for finding an ordinary king in a tournament, and the paper explicitly keeps this latter question open.
